name: Maya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a flatbed with a crane on the back for a builders' merchant, so blocks, timber, plasterboard, bags of cement, out to building sites and people doing up their houses. I load at seven, strap everything, and I'm usually doing six or seven drops. The best bit is the crane, honestly, swinging a pack of blocks over a hedge and setting it down exactly where the builder points. The worst bit is muddy sites where you're scared the truck's going to sink.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in this job, and how settled do you feel in it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I worked in the merchant's yard for three years on a forklift, then they paid half my truck licence if I stayed on. I've been driving just over a year, so I'm still the slowest on the crane and the lads tease me about it. I share a flat with my friend Jo, and I've got about two months of rent and bills saved, which feels good until January comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. Building sites still need someone to bring the stuff, and AI can't do that. Online I'd probably share a joke about all the money wasted on chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means the same worries I've already got. Winter is my real robot: every January the building sites go quiet and my hours drop from fifty to thirty, AI or no AI. That's two or three months on less money, and my savings get eaten every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and try to get properly good on the crane so I'm not first to lose hours. I'd also ask about weekend work at the merchant's other branch over winter. And I'd stop dipping into savings for holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat, really. Relieved about the AI, but the money worry stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a bad January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year I had three weeks of thirty-hour weeks and the rent didn't care. I used about a month of my savings and put off getting the car fixed. Jo lent me money once and I hated that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides who loses hours first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steve, the transport manager, and it's mostly who's quickest. That's why I practise the crane in the yard on quiet afternoons. I'm not quick yet, but I'm getting there.

say: I'd say building sites still need **deliveries**, and AI can't drive a crane lorry.
Online I'd joke about all the **money wasted** on chatbots.
think: My real threat is **winter**, when site work drops and hours fall to thirty.
Each January eats into my **two months** of savings, AI or no AI.
do: Practise the **crane** on quiet afternoons so I'm not first to lose hours.
Ask for **weekend shifts** at the other branch over winter.
feel: **Flat**: relieved about AI, but the winter money worry stays.
S0.quote: Winter is my real robot: every January the building sites go quiet and my hours drop from fifty to thirty, AI or no AI.
fieldNote: Maya's pressure is **seasonal hours**, which nothing in this scenario fixes.
She ties job security to **speed on the crane**, which she's still building.
Borrowing from her flatmate once left a mark; she hates **owing people**.

steps.text: Practise crane lifts in the yard on quiet afternoons
Ask for weekend shifts at the merchant's other branch in winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who should worry, not us. Then I'd say they deserve support too, because Pat on the trade counter has a mortgage. I'd probably share stuff about the union pushing for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The merchant's ordering desk will be a chatbot within a year, but no chatbot is lifting a pack of blocks over a fence on a muddy site. So I think I'm okay for a while. What worries me is that the software will plan our drops tighter, and the slowest driver on the crane looks bad on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try the new planning app properly once the other drivers say it works. I'd go to the union meeting the merchant's staff have twice a year, which I usually skip. And I'd keep saving through the summer so winter hurts less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm fine, but the people around me aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the slowest driver looks bad on a screen. What would that look like in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A screen in Steve's office with green and red times for each drop. If I'm red on the crane drops every week, I'm the one he moves to the small van or cuts in January. At the moment Steve knows I'm learning, but a screen doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the merchant would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat on the trade counter and the two women who do the orders over the phone. They know every builder by name. If a chatbot takes the orders, I'd lose the people who tell me which site has a nasty gate.

say: I'd say **office staff** should worry before drivers, and they deserve support too.
I'd share posts about the **union** pushing for training.
think: Ordering goes to a **chatbot**, but crane lifts on muddy sites stay with me for now.
Tighter **digital planning** makes the slowest crane driver look bad on a screen.
do: Try the **planning app** once other drivers say it works.
Attend the merchant's **union meeting**, which I usually skip.
Save more over **summer** so winter hurts less.
feel: **Uneasy**: I'm fine, but the people around me aren't.
S1.quote: The merchant's ordering desk will be a chatbot within a year, but no chatbot is lifting a pack of blocks over a fence on a muddy site.
fieldNote: Maya places the threat on the **office**, while her worry is being **timed** by software.
She values the order staff as her **source of site knowledge**.
Her steady style shows: she'll use the app only once **others prove** it.

steps.text: Use the new route-planning app once other drivers trust it
Go to the merchant staff's twice-yearly union meeting
Save extra over summer to cover January's short hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs governments to step in now, not after. Online I'd be angry, sharing stuff about taxing the companies that build these robots. At work I'd tell the lads we need the union to be loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the thinking stuff goes, so Steve's planning and all the ordering. The crane work lasts till about 2031. I'd be 32 when the robot cranes turn up, with two months of rent in the bank and a licence nobody wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to the union straight away and ask what they're doing for drivers. I'd look hard at the council's highways team, gritting and road repairs, because public jobs seem slower to change and they're unionised. I'd save harder too, maybe 250 a month by cutting the car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly. Like the floor tilting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time, but only if I start the minute I see it coming. I'd use it to get into a job that sits closer to people or the public. I don't know if that exists by 2031, but I'd rather be in it when the crane robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd cut the car. What does that change in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to get the early bus to the yard, which means leaving at half five. I'd stop seeing my mum on Sundays as much, because she's an hour out. That's the bit I'd hate.

say: I'd say **governments** need to step in now, not after the damage.
I'd push the lads to make the **union** loud.
think: Planning and ordering go in **2028**; the crane work lasts until around 2031.
At 32, I'd have **two months** of rent saved and a useless licence.
do: Ask the **union** straight away what it's doing for drivers.
Apply to the **council highways** team, where jobs seem slower to change.
Sell the car to save about **250 a month**.
feel: **Scared**, like the floor tilting under me.
S2.quote: I'd be 32 when the robot cranes turn up, with two months of rent in the bank and a licence nobody wants.
fieldNote: Maya expects to **lose driving work** around 2031 and says so plainly.
She sees **public-sector jobs** as slower and safer, and moves towards them.
The real cost she names is **Sunday visits** to her mother, not the car.

steps.text: Ask the union what it will do for crane drivers
Apply for a job on the council's highways team
Sell the car and save about 250 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, so let's use it, and the government should pay for retraining. I'd probably sign up for the union's education stuff and tell people about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031, robots around 2034, so I'd be 35. That's long enough to get really good at the crane and earn properly for a while. But I'd want something lined up by 2033 at the latest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get my lorry-loader crane ticket upgraded so I'm not the slow one any more. Then I'd look at a part-time course in site safety, because someone has to check robots on building sites. I'd keep saving through the summers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. It feels like there's a ladder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why site safety in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My cousin Rosa is a safety officer on big sites and she says nobody wants that job. If robots are on building sites, someone has to sign off that they won't drop a load on a person. I'd rather be that person than the one under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years ago you were in the yard on a forklift. What did that teach you about change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I can learn, just slowly. Everyone thought I'd give up on the crane and I didn't. If someone gives me five years, I'll get there.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** and the government should fund retraining.
I'd sign up for the **union's education** courses and spread the word.
think: Robots arriving around **2034** gives me time to get good and earn properly.
I'd want **something lined up** by 2033 at the latest.
do: Upgrade my **crane ticket** in the first year to stop being the slow one.
Start a part-time **site safety** course to check robots on building sites.
feel: **Anxious**, but with room to breathe, like there's a ladder.
S3.quote: If robots are on building sites, someone has to sign off that they won't drop a load on a person.
fieldNote: Five years turns Maya from **fear** into a step-by-step plan.
Her cousin's **safety role** gives her a concrete target.
Her confidence comes from proving people wrong on the **crane**.

steps.text: Upgrade the lorry-loader crane ticket in the first year
Start a part-time site safety course at night
Save through the busy summers for the winter dip

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the country to plan, so there's no excuse to leave people stranded. I'd say it calmly, though, not shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039, when I'm 40. I think by then there will have to be some kind of basic income or shorter weeks, because too many people would be out. I'd still want a skill, but I don't think I'd be on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the crane upgrade, then the site safety course over two or three years. I'd join the union's young members group and actually go. And I'd save for a deposit with Jo or a partner, because a home of my own matters more than a new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More like a long journey than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're counting on a basic income. What if it never comes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have the safety qualification and some savings, and I'd scrape by. But I honestly think if half the country's drivers and office workers are out, politicians would have to do something. People vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a girl starting in the yard today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get your tickets, all of them, and don't let anyone tell you the crane's not for you. Then learn something that means checking or teaching, not just doing. Doing is what the robots learn first.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuse** to leave people stranded.
I'd say it **calmly** to the lads in the yard, not shouting.
think: By 2039, I expect a **basic income** or shorter working weeks.
I'd still want a **skill**, but I wouldn't feel alone.
do: Finish the crane upgrade and **site safety** course over two or three years.
Join the union's **young members** group and actually attend.
Save for a home **deposit** instead of a new car.
feel: **Uneasy**, like a long journey rather than a cliff.
S4.quote: Get your tickets, all of them, and don't let anyone tell you the crane's not for you.
fieldNote: Maya's calm here rests on faith that **politics** will respond to mass job loss.
She shifts her savings goal to a **home deposit**, a sign of long-term thinking.
Her advice to younger women blends pride in the **crane** with realism.

steps.text: Finish the site safety course over two or three years
Join the union's young members group
Save for a flat deposit instead of a newer car

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because I'd be the slow driver with a crane licence and two months of rent. What would help is the union and the council getting together so drivers can move into public jobs, with the training paid.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in this trade. Being the only woman in the yard taught me to keep my head down and work, and I'm not sure keeping my head down works against a robot. It took me ages to be taken seriously in the yard. I worry the new jobs, the ones checking robots, will go to the same men who always get the good stuff.

headlineQuote: Being the only woman in the yard taught me to keep my head down and work, and I'm not sure keeping my head down works against a robot.
portrait: Maya Garcia, 27, drives a **crane flatbed** for a builders' merchant and is still the slowest on the crane.
Her steady worry is **winter hours**, which drain her two months of savings every January.
In the fast AGI picture she expects to lose driving work by 2031 and moves towards **council jobs**.
With more time she plans a **site safety** qualification and trusts politics to soften the blow.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be 32 with a crane licence and little savings.
whatWouldHelp: The **union and council** working together to move drivers into public jobs, with training paid.
